reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
clinicalPearls: Neuroendocrine tumours are a heterogeneous group arising most commonly in the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, and lungs, ranging from indolent well-differentiated tumours to highly aggressive neuroendocrine carcinomas
Tumour grade, based on proliferative markers such as mitotic count and Ki-67 index, is central to classifying behaviour and guiding treatment
Many are non-functioning and present late with mass effect or metastasis, while functioning tumours cause distinctive hormonal syndromes
The carcinoid syndrome, with flushing, diarrhoea, and wheeze, typically appears only once a midgut tumour has metastasised to the liver, allowing vasoactive mediators to bypass hepatic clearance
Chromogranin A is a widely used circulating marker, and urinary 5-HIAA supports the diagnosis of serotonin-secreting carcinoid tumours
Somatostatin receptor imaging, such as gallium-labelled PET, is valuable for localisation and staging and predicts response to somatostatin receptor-targeted therapy
Somatostatin analogues control hormonal symptoms and can slow tumour growth, and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy is an option for receptor-positive progressive disease

Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas behave like aggressive high-grade cancers and are treated with platinum-based chemotherapy, in contrast to the more indolent management of well-differentiated tumours
reference.pathophysiology: Neuroendocrine tumours originate from cells of the diffuse neuroendocrine system distributed throughout the body, which share the capacity to synthesise and secrete peptide hormones and biogenic amines. Well-differentiated tumours retain hormone production and receptor expression, including somatostatin receptors that are exploited for imaging and therapy, and generally grow slowly. Functioning tumours produce clinical syndromes through hormone excess, such as serotonin in carcinoid syndrome or insulin, gastrin, and other peptides from pancreatic tumours. Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas lose these features and behave aggressively with rapid proliferation and early metastasis. Some tumours occur within hereditary syndromes such as multiple endocrine neoplasia.
additionalDifferentials: Functional causes of flushing and diarrhoea, including mastocytosis and medullary thyroid carcinoma
Non-neuroendocrine primary tumours of the same organ
Pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma for catecholamine-related presentations
Irritable bowel syndrome or other benign causes of chronic diarrhoea
Hepatic metastases from other primary malignancies
additionalInvestigations: Histological grading with Ki-67 index and mitotic count to determine differentiation
Serum chromogranin A and, for suspected carcinoid, urinary 5-HIAA
Somatostatin receptor PET imaging for localisation and staging
Cross-sectional CT or MRI to assess primary tumour and metastatic burden
Specific hormone assays and evaluation for hereditary syndromes such as MEN when indicated
redFlags: Carcinoid crisis with severe flushing, haemodynamic instability, and bronchospasm, particularly around procedures
Rapidly progressive high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma with widespread metastases
Severe hormonal effects such as refractory hypoglycaemia from an insulinoma
Carcinoid heart disease with right-sided valve involvement in metastatic midgut tumours
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies widely by grade, differentiation, site, and stage; well-differentiated low-grade tumours can be compatible with prolonged survival even with metastases, whereas poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas have an aggressive course and poor outcome.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal-appearing indolent tumour is benign and underestimating metastatic potential
Failing to prevent carcinoid crisis with somatostatin analogue cover before surgery or interventions
Managing high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma as if it were an indolent tumour
Overlooking an associated hereditary syndrome that alters surveillance and family screening
references: DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
management: Surgical resection is the only potentially curative approach for localised well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours and should be pursued when medically feasible.

For pancreatic NETs, resection is favored for functional or symptomatic tumours and for non-functioning tumours 2 cm or larger, while small non-functioning tumours can reasonably be observed with interval imaging.

Resectable pulmonary carcinoid is managed surgically, with stereotactic ablative radiotherapy considered for non-surgical candidates and adjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy considered for nodal involvement, aggressive histology, or incomplete resection.
Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide or lanreotide are first line for progressive metastatic well-differentiated NET and also help control hormonal symptoms.
Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy with a radiolabeled somatostatin analogue is an option for somatostatin-receptor-positive disease progressing on a somatostatin analogue.
mTOR-directed therapy with everolimus, alone or combined with a somatostatin analogue, is an approved option for progressive NET including pulmonary and pancreatic primaries.
Cytotoxic chemotherapy, including regimens combining an alkylating agent with capecitabine, has a role in more aggressive or bulky pancreatic and pulmonary NET.
Checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy is investigational for well-differentiated NET and not an established standard of care.
Liver-directed therapies such as resection, ablation, or embolisation are used for liver-dominant metastatic disease.
Asymptomatic patients with low-volume, slowly progressive disease can be followed with active surveillance before starting systemic therapy.
Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma is managed with platinum-based chemotherapy rather than the somatostatin-analogue or mTOR-inhibitor pathway used for well-differentiated tumours.

Carcinoid syndrome is treated first with somatostatin analogues, with telotristat as an add-on for diarrhea not controlled by dose escalation, alongside bile-acid binders, pancreatic enzymes, antibacterial therapy, and anti-motility agents as needed.
Perioperative somatostatin analogue cover is standard before procedures in carcinoid syndrome to prevent carcinoid crisis, and adrenergic agents should be avoided if a crisis develops.
Patients with carcinoid heart disease should have baseline and periodic echocardiographic screening and early referral to cardiology and cardiac surgery for valve disease.
